questions.q: Why is it inaccurate to describe the Chapter 1 incident as an unplanned detour from this capstone's real work?
options: Because the incident didn't actually involve real data

Because building a multi-AZ Kubernetes cluster and a FinOps dashboard with cost visibility was specifically meant to make a moment like this survivable and diagnosable — the incident proved that value, it didn't interrupt it
Because the incident was scripted from the start of the course materials
Because the cluster was rebuilt from scratch after the incident
questions.explain: The architecture's whole value proposition — per-AZ visibility, a disciplined root-cause process — was proven, not interrupted, by the incident actually happening.

questions.q: What does this Advanced capstone add that the Beginner and Intermediate tiers of the same path did not reach?
options: Nothing — all three tiers are identical in scope
A full Kubernetes platform, two clouds working together, a cross-functional incident with real leadership stakes, and a hardening phase after the fix
A switch to a completely different fictional company
The removal of Terraform from the stack entirely
questions.explain: The Beginner tier migrated one app; the Intermediate tier added containers, CI/CD, and a backup cloud; this Advanced tier reaches full multi-cloud Kubernetes scale with a real incident and its aftermath.

questions.q: Which of the following is named as a real, deliberately out-of-scope extension a senior Cloud Architect might add next?
options: Automated, recurring chaos engineering instead of one scheduled drill, and a true multi-region active-active architecture instead of a secondary-cloud failover target
Removing the FinOps dashboard since the incident is already resolved
Deleting the incident report now that the platform is hardened
Reverting topologySpreadConstraints now that the ceiling has been raised
questions.explain: Automated chaos engineering, multi-region active-active architecture, and automatic cost-anomaly detection are all named as honest, deliberate scope boundaries — not mistakes.

questions.q: What real-world career progression does this capstone's skill set map onto?
options: There is no real career path connected to this work
Cloud Engineer, toward Senior Cloud Engineer or Site Reliability Engineer, toward Cloud Architect, toward Principal or Staff Cloud Architect
Directly into an unrelated field such as graphic design
A path that requires no further certification or demonstrated experience of any kind
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly names this progression, along with certifications like AZ-305, the CKA, and the FinOps Foundation's practitioner certification as ways to validate pieces of it.

questions.q: What is the single most important thing this capstone's second half (Lessons 19-26) demonstrated, beyond simply fixing the original bug?
options: That Kubernetes should never be used for e-commerce workloads

That hardening a platform after an incident — auditing for similar blind spots, resolving stakeholder conflicts with real data, and validating everything together — is where a senior engineer's work actually diverges from a junior fix
That cost and reliability can never both be satisfied at once
That documentation should always be written before any testing happens
questions.explain: The entire second half of the capstone was built to show that fixing one bug and genuinely hardening a platform against the next one are different, both-necessary pieces of real senior-level work.
